# Is the Market Rally Broadening?


Stocks, as measured by the S&P 500, are up over 13% through early August. The solid gains have been fueled by a resilient economy, steady consumer spending, optimism around artificial intelligence and better-than-expected earnings growth. Still, some investors worry the advance may be too concentrated in technology and AI-capex monetization may fall short of expectations. A closer look suggests that it is not just tech moving the market higher.


Enlarge


With technology companies on track to deliver a roughly 50% earnings growth rate in 2026, it is not surprising that the sector has remained a major driver of market performance. However, market gains are not solely reliant on technology and AI-linked names. Excluding these, the S&P 500 is still posting solid gains of 8% year to date, which is a healthy sign and indicative of broader market strength.


A key measure of market breadth is the comparison between the market-cap weighted S&P 500 and the equal-weighted S&P 500. It may surprise some investors to learn that the equal-weighted S&P 500 Index is modestly outperforming the S&P 500 so far this year, with a gain of 14% versus 13.2% through early August. This suggests areas beyond technology and AI capex beneficiaries are contributing to moving the market higher.


Another way to evaluate whether the market is broadening is to look at how many stocks are trading above their recent trend. Currently, about 72% of S&P 500 companies are trading above their 200-day moving average. That is the highest level since December 2024.


Collectively, these measures suggest that breadth is improving – a constructive sign for the forward outlook.

The recent one-day equity selloff reflected weaker sentiment amid election uncertainty and concerns that slower artificial intelligence spending could weigh on growth and earnings. Still, pullbacks of this magnitude have often been followed by solid returns, and we remain constructive given the economy’s resilience and AI’s long-term potential.

When it comes to investing, time matters. While headlines and short-term perspectives can lead investors to try to time the market, investors have historically been rewarded by playing the long game. Rather than overreacting to market noise, investing over longer time periods can help smooth the ride without sacrificing returns. The lesson: stay diversified and invested for the long term.

[Contained Contagion?](https://www.bny.com/wealth/global/en/insights/chart-of-the-week/contained-contagion.html)


U.S. high yield credit spreads have widened year to date, reflecting greater investor caution about perceived default risk. The move also raises concerns about possible credit contagion. However, because spread widening has been concentrated in the lowest-quality issuers rather than higher-quality issuers, we don’t anticipate broader market stress.


Article | Chart of the Week


[Can the Bull Run in Corporate Margins Continue?](https://www.bny.com/wealth/global/en/insights/chart-of-the-week/can-the-bull-run-in-corporate-margins-continue.html)


Higher inflation and elevated interest rates typically weigh on corporate profitability, yet corporate margins continue to climb to record highs. While that strength is evident both in the U.S. and abroad, U.S. outperformance versus Europe is now the widest on record. Stronger margins have helped contribute to better-than-expected earnings and reinforce U.S. equity leadership. The question now is whether that strength can persist.
